utterances.text: Then you see down underneath --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says: "General hospital in Trebinje" up in the corner.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: That is what I was going to ask you. The one on the right says: "The General Hospital of Trebinje" and the one on the left says: "The War Hospital of Boracko Jezero", does it not. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a hospital up in Boracko Jezero but I don't know to whom it belonged. Somebody gave me referral for the surgery but they didn't perform a surgery on me until my disability had been established.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am not asking you about that. On the left it says: "The War Hospital of Boracko Jezero" and on the right it says: "The Medical Centre of Trebinje". Now those two cities are at least four hours away, are they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are far apart from one another. I don't know who ran that hospital. I only know that I went to Trebinje to get surgery. However the surgeon asked me whether your disability has been established, and I said "no". Then he said: "Well, don't do it now", because then he won't be able to prove it later. Then I asked to be given surgery in Belgrade. They said not yet but I think I will do it once I go back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, these doctors were all Serbian doctors, who knew about your criminal case here in The Hague, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not know. They have no idea about this.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Then can your Honour please turn it to the second page, where the doctor, the same visit, writes a little further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a referral for examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a referral for examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The next page says -- and the doctor whose name we cannot ascertain said that you sustained injuries at the enemy detention camp of Celebici three years ago. Is that not what that says on the back of your original document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it does, because my injuries were sustained in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So the only thing he is putting down there is what you told him; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told him that I needed a surgery and I already explained why they didn't want to perform a surgery, because I needed to establish my disability.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So he referred you to other doctors, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Trebinje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: When he makes a finding that you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, to another doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because up in Jezero there was -- I could only have done it in Trebinje, but now I have started the process to get a surgery in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Mr Gotovac, I am very aware that you need some medical attention for your condition, but my question here is: this doctor is a referring doctor, and what he wrote down on this document is just what you told him. He does not have any personal knowledge about this enemy detention camp at Celebici that he wrote down, does he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He said: "Where did you get it?" I said: "I got it in 1992 in Celebici under torture."

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: This Doctor Butalja, he is a Serbian doctor, is he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't ask him and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then could you pick up the second document, where nobody has a translation of this, but there is no -- the second document that talks about your hand injury, there is no date on this, is there, Mr Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot see one no, there isn't one.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, other than what you tell us, we have no way to tell whether this was even written by a doctor, do we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was written by a doctor; in fact, by three doctors. It was signed by three doctors, so that I can undergo surgery in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And those doctors are through the Belgrade Serbian Commission that you went to see; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got this in Visegrad from doctors there. I don't know if they were Serbian. I was not asking. I just wanted to undergo surgery and to go here and on my way back to have surgery, and they signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr Gotovac, excuse me. You did not go to these doctors to have surgery on your hand, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Belgrade no, no. When I go there now, I will ask to have surgery first for one thing and then for the other, and then to see what can be done about my shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, the truth is you got this document two months ago before testifying in this court, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one about my hand?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I got it 15 days before I was supposed to travel here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is even shorter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't even think that I would be handing this document here. I just wanted to have my surgery done in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have no further questions about these two documents, your Honour. I would just like to argue as to why I do not believe they should be admitted into evidence. Thank you, Mr Gotovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: These are his documents. Let us exhibit them. You can argue about the reliability or the probative value later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for allowing me to question him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me find out just one question: was it possible for you to get any certificate of your injury at the Celebici camp, room 22 at the medical facilities there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Why? Because you were examined by doctors there and they treated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These doctors were prisoners. They were also in detention. They couldn't have issued any documents to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: They were functioning as doctors for the infirmary there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they were detainees themselves. Both doctors will testify before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr Greaves, I think you are satisfied with what has transpired. You do not need further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think we have got the answer and I am grateful to your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I get my English translation there, and if you would like, I imagine that the prosecution could make some copies of that to provide you for the record. I am sorry. I have a few markings on there. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you were that charitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can give us cleaner copies. It does not matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, the prosecutor -- I think you are making a joint application about this witness being examined by a doctor to indicate whether he was injured or, if he was, how long ago, whether any of his injuries are the result of what happened when he was in the Celebici camp. I think these are your enquiries.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I think we both would like to know the truth of whatever has happened to Mr Gotovac, and I think that is the best way to find out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. The Trial Chamber will grant the application. I think we will make the necessary reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that all you have for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That is all we have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The defence has nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Nothing from us, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. This witness is discharged, pending his examination by the doctor, his medical examination. It will make it easier for everyone if he is examined before he leaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go to the next witness, that just brings to mind that the court had ordered an examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. (Witness withdrew from court)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The court had ordered an examination of Mirko Babic too. I was just wondering if we had any results of this examination yet so we might be provided with a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. We will communicate to you, because I hear this examination actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Who is your next witness that you want to call now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We now call Mr Mirko Kuljanin as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is he related to the woman -- Mrs Cecez was referring to some women who were brought to Celebici camp. She named four women and one was, I think, Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: There are many Kuljanins anyway in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a common name. Okay. She mentioned four of them, Melina and others. One was Kuljanin. I was wondering whether he was related to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The surname Kuljanin is very, very spread, actually. We have a number of persons with this surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please swear the witness. MR MIRKO KULJANIN (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): Is that all right? Can I sit down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirko Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: What is your date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 26th October 1931.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say what is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Bradina, Konjic municipality, the village of Bradina, the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Kuljanin, what education did you receive? I mean, what kind of schools did you attend and how many years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had eight years of primary school and then I had some exams that were for my work, the work that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: What is this work, your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked for the rail roads. I was a conductor in Sarajevo, conductor on the trains.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Where did you live at the beginning of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Bradina, in the village of Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Were you still working as a railroad conductor at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was retired since 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can you say, was Bradina a village with Serbian majority or Muslim majority or Croatian majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Serb majority, almost all Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how many inhabitants or how many families did Bradina have at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 600, 600 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how many of them were Serbs and how many Muslims and how many Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I know is by households, the people who owned property there. There were four families of Croats and the rest were all Serbs. There were a few Muslims, but those were the people who worked there, and they lived there temporarily, so I don't know if we counted a single household as Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say what is approximately the distance between Bradina and Konjic town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 12, 13 kms, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could ask now that witness Kuljanin be provided with Prosecution Exhibit number 4, please, which is a map, and could the map be placed on the ELMO, please, Prosecution Exhibit number 4. Mr Kuljanin, if you watch this map on your right, could you indicate to the court the position of the town of Konjic and the position of the village of Bradina on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is Konjic and this is Bradina. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: You should indicate that on the map not in front of you but on your right please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Probably the map has to be shown more completely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Konjic. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And Bradina. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In the whitish area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is Bradina situated on a road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: In which direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The road from Sarajevo through Konjic towards Mostar and towards the coast leads through Bradina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not sure the defence will allow if you ask leading questions in respect of this direction. Where is Bradina? Which direction is it from Konjic? Do not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you state again: is Bradina, with respect to Konjic, in which direction is that situated coming from Konjic; you go in which direction through Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Konjic to Bradina is in the direction of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Kuljanin was there a time when Bradina was affected by armed conflict in 1992, I mean affected by real military action, or shooting or shelling or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that much. There was something on May 25th to 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there a time when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested on 26th May in the afternoon towards the evening with a larger group of other people.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you briefly say -- explain the circumstances of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I reluctantly remember this. I do not like to recall that day and everything that happened then, but I know that it was horrible, that it was not part of human relationships. Whatever was -- whoever was in that village, in that hamlet was going to be annihilated, not just people but the livestock as well, and then everything was being set on fire, the houses and barns and all the other structures, and that's when I had the most stress. I heard the screams, not just human ones but from the livestock, the cows that were burning alive in barns and dogs and cats.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, can you describe the very moment of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a group of women and children with whom I was herded onto that road that led to Konjic. I arrived there with the last of the group. There was a lot of people there. I don't know the exact number. They were already lined up. It was a long column.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr Kuljanin, where were you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at home when they came, when this group arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Which group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how to call them. Army? They had uniforms on, mostly black uniforms. There was some camouflage, multi-coloured uniform, but for the most part it was black uniform. Now who this military was I wouldn't know. Who commanded I don't know either, because, I am sorry, from that group I did not know a single person.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Well, how many people were they, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many. There were a lot of people in the village so there were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: You said they came into your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: You said you were in your house when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Could you explain very briefly how did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was sad. We could hear shooting from different sides and then they started coming, and a relative and I found a white rag to have it ready. We didn't know what to expect. Then we saw them around the village, and then they started coming to the village. Then they arrived in the village, and then this sad scene took place when they entered the village and started their acts.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Please, Mr Kuljanin I would like you to tell us exactly how were you arrested personally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my home. On one side there were women and children and on the other side there were four or five men and I was in front of my house. My father was in the house. He was 84, and I was -- I had been with him. I saw the four or five younger ones. They tied their hands behind their backs. I was there with this group where they were tying people up. A man came, a soldier, and asked me where my pistol was. I had that pistol with the permit, and I looked at him and he seemed to know that I had this pistol. Then I went into the house and I said: "It's not here. You know where you keep it. You don't keep it where it's accessible to kids." Then I went into the bedroom where I gave him my pistol. When we came out, the ones that were there were already led on, and then they included me in the group with women and children, and there were also four elderly men, and this group was then taken down to Bradina. Then we stood there and then they put us in a column that was already lined up and ready and facing Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, were you told the reason why you were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing. I was told nothing. I did not know, nor did I ever find out. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did you in any way take part in the defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not directly, even though I did have a rifle, I had it before, a regular rifle. I had the property up there and it was already sensitive, and there was a younger man also with me, so that he and I went to plant potatoes and then we put down the rifles and we started working, but there was a group right around us and asked for a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr Kuljanin. You are now talking of something which took place in some other time, not the day of your arrest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. That was before. I don't know exactly when, maybe 15 days before that, and at that time I was -- that rifle was taken away from me. That was a group also.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: So since you have been talking about this rifle now, if you want to explain now who gave you that rifle, about fifteen days before your arrest you said, if I am not wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at that time it was taken away from me and I had been given it five or six days prior to that by Slobodan Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Who took that away from you five or six days after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were some people. I don't know where from. I didn't know them but I think that they came from the village of Repovci, from that direction. There were seven or eight of them, and I knew some of them by sight, but I didn't know them by their names.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: So at the time of your arrest you didn't have any other weapon besides your pistol in your bedroom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Going back to this day of your arrest, can you approximately say how many persons in your village were armed and active in the defence of the village of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, but I could not say that it was an active defence, because I know there were very few, maybe 20, 25 people there and defence was nothing. It was just people trying to defend their houses and families, and given the forces there, there was no defence, because if it was also known that none of the people who attacked were -- did any harm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr Turone. We will have to rise and come back about 4.20 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: -- for you to continue. (4.00 pm) (Short break) (4.20 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please let us have the witness and carry on. (Witness returned to court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please warn the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You can carry on, Mr Turone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. So, Mr Kuljanin, what happened to you right after your arrest? I mean, where were you brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they took us down there, the whole group, women, children, all of us together, the women and children were separated to one side and we, the men, were lined up in the column. We stood there for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: What do you mean "there"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean at the crossroads, at the road, where the column was lined up to head to Konjic. We were lined up one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: You mean still in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. After that where were you brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we stood there for a time. Some more people were gathered there and then we got the order to take off our coats, hats, and we had to comply. Then the order was issued to start walking, and we had to be as close to each other as possible, and we had to keep our hands behind our heads, and so we set off down that road towards Konjic. Then they started beating us. We did not know -- I did not know what was going on. I could not believe that this was happening and we went for maybe 2 kms, but the soldiers were all the time on both sides of the column, and they beat us. Men were covered in blood. Their heads were broken. They fell down. We were hit with various objects. Some people were barefoot because their shoes fell off. Then we came to a tunnel, which had been blown up. This was done by some people from Konjic. The tunnel was blown up and closed for traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Which tunnel are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tunnel on the road from Bradina to Konjic. I think it is about two kms approximately away from Bradina, from the centre of Bradina on the route to Konjic, and when we came there, those who had already been there, they were put on trucks, and they had already gone. I remember very clearly that I was in the last vehicle. It was a tonne truck but en route we were beaten very severely and my head was broken in several places. I was bleeding so hard that I couldn't even see where I was going, but he continued beating me and told me to keep my hands up. So I managed somehow to get down. So when we had to get on we could not do it, because we were so weak from the beating, and a man fell down, and I saw when he was killed. I was behind him. He couldn't get up because of the beating. I don't know how to explain. He was a fat man. He couldn't get up. His name was Drago Kuljanin and he was killed there. So when we got to the vehicle, I know that I left this place in the last vehicle. It was a tonne truck. I tried to wipe the blood away from my eyes, but the guard would not let me and he beat me. So we reached Konjic. They took us to Musala sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment, Mr Kuljanin. So you reached Konjic in a truck you said. How many prisoners were together with you in that same truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe about 15, I think. It was a smaller truck and the others had left before. I remember clearly that I was in the last vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: How do you know that you were in the last vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because there were no other vehicles behind us but I was really very severely beaten en route from Bradina to that tunnel and many other people were beaten too, so I couldn't get on, and that caused more beating, so that somebody may even have helped me to get on. So when we came to Konjic they, as I said, brought us to the sports hall, and when we got off the trucks, we were beaten again.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean the sports hall, Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: How many trucks did transport other prisoners before your truck left? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I couldn't tell you. I don't know how many trucks there were.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Still do you have specific knowledge of other trucks having left before yours? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know. I learned later from the other people when we all got together in Celebici. I heard from them that there were some people in the trucks that were at the head of the column, that they never went to the sports hall in Musala, but were transferred to Celebici directly. I don't know what the reason was for our transportation there. Maybe because we were to be beaten. Maybe there was beating there. Maybe we had to wait until everything down there was ready for us. I don't know. My idea is that maybe because of our large numbers they wouldn't have been able to do everything that they had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, how long did you stop in Musala? How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an exact answer, but I think an hour, maybe a bit more, approximately, and I can tell you that when we got off the trucks, as we entered the corridor, I noticed a dead body lying there and blood. There was no light. I learned later that this was the body of Petko Mrkajic, Petko. Fortunately or unfortunately I was in a unit or a group right at the beginning which was in charge of water, and I had the chance to have a drink of water several times, and to wipe my eyes and I was able to regain consciousness. Then later when we spent some time there we were once again called to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: You mean by "there" where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside the sports hall, near the entrance. There was a vehicle there. It was no longer the tonne truck in which I had been transported from the tunnel in Bradina to Konjic. It was a van, some kind of a van.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, after staying about one hour in Musala sports hall where were you brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were again taken out and put on a van, and we travelled on. I didn't know where we were. I didn't have any ideas where they were taking us. I thought that they would take us to some kind of a gorge or to the Jablanica lake to be killed or some holes. I didn't know the Celebici area. I didn't know what was waiting for us there, what was waiting for the people who were taken there. So when we reached Celebici again I didn't know that place, because I was not in a position to know anything about the place. This was a military installation. So I didn't know anything about the place.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, can you say approximately at what time did you arrive at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not during the day. It was at night. I think it was after midnight. It was already very dark when we set off from Bradina, and then we had to go to Konjic, and then we waited there and travelled to Celebici. So I think it was after midnight. I don't know the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: So do you mean the night between 26th and 27th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to 27th May.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Were you transported to Celebici in the same truck in which you arrived at Musala?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No, it was a van.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Van, I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The first one was a tonne truck en route to Konjic and from Konjic it was a van. It was a closed-type vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: How many prisoners were together with you in this van, which transported you to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were about eight or nine of us, as far as I can remember. I was a bit confused, but that's what I think. When we reached Celebici, we were still inside the van, but we could hear the screams and moans next to a wall. People were beaten there, beaten very severely. Then they were thrown into the tunnel Number 9. That's what they called it.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, let me ask you: where were these people moaning from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the van -- our van had already arrived there to that place in Celebici, and we could hear the moans from the outside, and then our turn came. The van was opened and we were told to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, how do you know that the other trucks or vans taking other prisoners to Celebici did not stop in Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I heard from the people who were in that group, because later on we somehow communicated with each other in one way or another. Some people from one group would say: "No, we did not go to Konjic", and those who did go to Konjic, we knew about them.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Were these people whose moaning you heard at the arrival of your van people from Bradina too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All the people there at the time were from Bradina but I don't know how many vehicles, how many trucks there were, but all of them were there. Later on, the next day, the day after that, when we managed to see each other, we saw that all of us from Bradina were there, although it wasn't very easy to see, but we did learn that, and then, when we were transferred from the Number 9 to number 6, we realised that all of us who were driven from Bradina on the night of 26th, that we were all there. I heard those screams and moans. As I got off, I couldn't get off very easily, so I slid down from the van, and I fell down, and by accident I found -- I saw that there was something shiny, a shiny metal object. It was a nail.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Where was this nail, Mr Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was lying on the ground. Maybe it fell off one of the vehicles or maybe it was just there. At any rate I found it, and I thought that I should somehow commit suicide. I took this nail and my head was cut in several places, and I placed the nail inside my wound and I tried to push it inside my head in order to commit suicide, but I didn't manage to do so. As I lay down on the ground, somebody hit me in the back, and he noticed this and he said: "Look what he's been trying to do", and I thought that maybe somebody would hit that nail and thus ease my suffering for ever, but nobody did that, and I just heard that somebody said: "Look what this guy tried to do." So they hit me several times, two or three times, and they pulled me inside the building Number 9, the tunnel. This concludes the events of that night as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, can you say approximately the total number of prisoners from Bradina who were transported to Celebici that night with those trucks or vans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately 80-100. I don't know exactly, but I think maybe 80-100. It was a long column. I saw that when we were lined up there in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: You mean -- lined up in Bradina you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Bradina when we were lined up standing one behind the other.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Arriving at Celebici, where exactly inside the camp did this beating you have been talking about happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The worst beating was from Bradina to the tunnel. This was the hardest time for me, because this was when I fell down from the blows and got up again. All the beatings were really incredible, the objects that they used, and it seemed to me as if they had prepared for that. They had all kinds of objects that they used to beat us and the worst beating that I took was when I was hit with a rifle barrel in my left side and I thought that I had been run through. I fell down and I somehow managed to get up again.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr Kuljanin. My question -- I understand that. My question was concerning the moment when you arrived at Celebici, right after you got out of your truck, and you found that nail. You told us that you saw people there and there was some beating there too, and my question was: where exactly inside the camp did that happen right after your arrival there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the camp compound next to a wall, next to a concrete wall. People were lined up against that wall with their hands up, and then that night there was again this beating. As I told you, my group, we were still in the van, and when we heard the moans of those ahead of us, when they were beaten, and then our turn came.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: How far was that wall from the entrance of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it's not very far, maybe -- I don't know the exact distance.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the wall itself is quite long, and it abuts the building Number 9. I don't know if it goes all the way down to the entrance gate.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, in the very moment when you got out of your van, can you say, approximately how many prisoners did you say were already lined up against the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a group of maybe fifteen of them, but it was -- people were going there group by group, probably as vehicles came in and unloaded one group, then they brought in another group. This is the way I figured it out.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: You say that these people were from Bradina too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did you recognise anybody in that group you saw lined up against the wall right in the very moment when you got out of your van?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't really feel like looking. If I was in any condition to see, I would be able to recognise them. My only thought was to end my suffering, to commit suicide. I saw those people. They were all facing the wall. Some fell down and then got up again. I don't know what had happened to them, but I do know that horrible things happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Going back to the nail you drove into your head --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Attempted to drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you attempt to drive this nail into your head or did you actually drive that into your head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My intention was to do that. Maybe if I had had some kind of an object, maybe a stone, I think I maybe would have, but I could only -- I only tried to do that with my hand and I failed. I would have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say how long was this nail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember it wasn't very long. It was a small nail. It's classified as 6 or 7. It wasn't very long.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, approximately how long were you personally beaten in this situation at the wall inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was not really beaten, because I was already unable to stand. Maybe they hit me three times. Somebody hit me three times, and then some people pulled me inside. I was not beaten really severely there. My most severe beating was en route from Bradina to the tunnel and when we were getting on the vehicle. This is where I was beaten very badly, and again when we got off in Konjic, and when we got inside the corridor in the sports hall. This is where I was beaten. Again let me remind you, if it hadn't been for the water and I think that the other people around me, they helped me, and they wiped my face and rubbed my neck, and I think it helped me. Then when I was taken inside Number 9, in the morning a man showed up at the door. I was very close, because I was the last one in the group to enter, so I was close to the door. The man showed up. It wasn't daylight yet, and he shone a flashlight over us, and he cursed our mothers, and he said -- he cursed and he said: "Who did this to these people? Who beat and tortured them so badly?" I didn't know anyone. I didn't know who he was. Then he called out the doctor, Relja Mrkajic. He told him to get out. He called Simo Zelenovic and I think Simo's brother. I don't recall his name, and they got out. They didn't go back. I asked for some water and Simo brought me some water. So I had a good drink of water and I got down on the concrete, and it wasn't actually very bad to lie down on the concrete. I lay down on my left side, which was hurting very badly, and after a while I noticed that the day was breaking, that it was dawn. Then some other man came. Again I don't know who he was. I didn't know anyone. He looked at us. He told some of us to get out. He pointed a finger at me, because I was again covered in blood. He told us to go somewhere for our wounds to be bandaged or something like that. I don't know. This is what happened. We went there, but it wasn't really very much. I just wanted -- I just asked them to allow me to wipe my eyes. They didn't let me. There were some nurses there and they -- I had two cuts, two large cuts on my head and they put some plasters, band aids, on it, and they took us back to the tunnel Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, do you have any specific direct knowledge of the physical consequences which any other prisoner suffered after that particular beating at the wall on the night of your arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that very few of us didn't have any consequences. I think that everybody had some consequences, but some had more serious and some had less serious. Those of us who had been hit on the head, it was the easiest to notice those injuries. If you had injuries on other parts of the body, it wasn't so noticeable. I know how it was with me. My left side was completely black because of the blows that I sustained, but you couldn't -- the bruises, they lasted for a month maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you mention the name of any other person from that group about whom you might have seen some visible bruises or some consequences anyway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I remember Vukasin Mrkajic very well. Both his eyes were shut the morning when we were called out. That man could not see. His eyes were both shut from the blows. I remember him the best, but there were many others.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Was Vukasin Mrkajic in the same van with you arriving at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He must have been up front. I did not see him until the next day when I saw him, when I noticed him.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever find out when the first trucks or vans arrived to Celebici from Bradina that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact time I would not be able to tell, but if I take into account the stops, and we did stop my vehicle, the vehicle where I was in -- I am sorry -- we stopped a little bit longer up there at that tunnel after we had climbed in, and somehow the engine wouldn't start. So the other vehicles had put in some distance between us. So I think it would have been, plus with the stoppage in Konjic, maybe two hours. At least an hour and a half; maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say how far tunnel 9 was from the wall where the beating took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't far. It was almost next to the wall, as far as I can recall. It was close, close to the wall, not far to that tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, you see a kind of a model in front of you. Do you recognise what this model represents? This big model in front of you, do you see it? You can stand up and look in front of you. Do you see anything there in front of you? Do you have an idea of what this model is representing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess that is the Celebici military installation which was then turned into the camp. That should be it.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to provide the witness with something to point out the details in this model, and if you are comfortable, Mr Kuljanin, you can move around, because I would like you to -- if you are in a position to do that, could you indicate on that model the places you have been talking about so far, I mean the entrance, the wall and what you called tunnel Number 9. Could you provide the witness with any microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This should be the gate here. (Indicating). Speak in there? That is the entrance and then this was -- this building was the building and I think this must have been the command of the military at the time. (Indicating). This is what was called the number 22. This is what it should be. This was also some building that was used for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: What about the wall you have been talking about and tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up here, this is where it should be. (Indicating). This should be Number 9, I think, as far as I can understand, because I was not there much. That should be the wall there around Number 9. As far as I could recall, this is how it should look. The gate, but I don't recall this. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr Kuljanin. Mr Kuljanin, when you entered tunnel 9, approximately how many prisoners were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All those who were brought in that night were put there, were put there. We were pretty much packed. I remember well that tunnel even though I was not there very long. It had a sort of a drop. It went downhill. I remember the best that after two or three days people had to relieve themselves and some of them had to defecate and they were not able to be taken anywhere. Then everybody went to urinate down at the bottom, and after a while it started smelling. They rarely open up the doors, only when they needed to. There was some small bar or some grates and so people had trouble with the stench, and then I also noticed that people found relief on concrete because of the beatings that they received, because it was cold.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, was there any light inside the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no light. If somebody would come, they would point the flashlight, and that was the only light.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean the darkness was complete, or could you see something inside the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost total darkness. You can't see almost anything and especially at night. During day-time you could see maybe a little bit but at night-time the dark was absolute.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Were you in a position during day-time with the coarse light inside to see the traces of the bruises on other people you have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to the leading form of the question. He has not talked about bruises on anybody but himself. He is putting words in the witness' mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought he did. Anyway were those people inside the tunnel familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, almost all of them. However, I could not -- they were not very visible to me. We had no possibility of moving around much. It was very narrow from one end to the other, and, beaten as we were with injuries, people moved only if they had to, if they had to go down to the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, how can you say "how beaten we were"? How could you see that inside the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew -- I felt from as much as I was able to walk and to move, and my head was cut and my left side hurt. I had problems breathing and I had problems turning, turning over. So I was able to notice, and then I -- when I went back to Musala and Konjic I knew more, but that is coming. Then I also had a lacerated lip, and I asked if they could treat it, but nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, could you find out in that first night in which conditions, in which physical conditions were the other people inside the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He could not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. He could not see, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How would he know what physical condition they were?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But he has been talking about the conditions of people inside. So I would like to ask him how could he find out anything about these conditions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only condition he has talked about is his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Well, he heard moans of the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Crying. There were some people injured probably. So the learned counsel is trying to find out if he was in a position to see their injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: As far as seeing, I believe the question was asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The witness has said about people moaning there, so you can ask. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I have an objection to interpretation. When he talked about a lacerated lip, he said that he wanted it cut off, and the interpretation said to have it treated, so I would like the interpretation reviewed later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The treatment has not yet come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Did you understand the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I did not actually. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is one of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can prove that. I can prove that right away from inside of my upper lip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now what Mr Brackovic was complaining of was that the request of the witness was that the lip should be cut off. Is that what he said, not that it should be treated. It should be cut off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The inside -- MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): I asked that the interpretation be compared to the transcript. I will follow it very carefully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please let the interpretation be properly corrected. Repeat your objection so it can be interpreted, so that it will appear in the transcript. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, when the witness said he had a lacerated lip which bothered him he said that he asked for it to be cut off, but it was interpreted in another way. Instead of saying "cut off", the expression "treat" was used, and I think it's not a proper interpretation of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is quite appropriate. Actually his evidence was indicating the stress in which he was, and not the interpretation. Mr Turone, you can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So, Mr Kuljanin, when you entered the tunnel and found other people there, you were in a condition to see, take knowledge of, how did they feel physically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not well at all. People said to one another "it hurts", but we were all packed and everybody was using these words, that they were in pain, that they were beaten up. Some people had fractures, but can I say something about this lip?

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Of course you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. My lip was not lacerated so that I asked for the lip to be cut off. The inside was injured and it was from the inside, so that was bothering me, and that's what I had in mind, not that my lip be cut off, and there's still a scar there. So I had a laceration on the inside and it bothered me. That's what I had in mind. That's what I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe briefly the physical characteristics of tunnel 9 inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the length. I know that it was narrow, maybe 1.5 metres in width, and it was completely dark, and in concrete. I don't know what its military purposes were. So that it was really uncomfortable, especially the stench and taste and whatever -- mostly the stench for what people had to use it for.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever reach the bottom of this tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall I had to go to urinate about twice, and there already there was a puddle that was created from people who were going there to relieve themselves, so that there was a terrible stench there. I had to go there a couple of times. We often asked to be taken out, but they would not allow that. So then we had to go down all the way to the gate, to the exit, so that people were forced. So then we were stepping on one another and they said: "Don't step on my foot", or something. So you did it only if you really had to.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how long did you stay in tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. It wasn't that long. Some five days, I think I was there, four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did the number of prisoners in Number 9 change in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. A group arrived and then we were transferred to number 6. As far as I know, all of us from Number 9 moved to number 6 and the group which arrived was put in Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr Kuljanin,. My question was not this one. I mean: in those days during which you stayed in tunnel 9, did the number of prisoners change? Did anybody go or come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall that anybody came, only what I mentioned, that this man who took out three people that same morning, 27th, the doctor and Zelenovic, Simo, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did you stay in a particular place inside tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were put there, I was near the door because I was one of the last in, so I was closer to the entrance than to the middle or the end.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you say something about supplies of food and drinking water during those days in Number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The following day I don't know if anybody was giving us anything, but we asked for water, so we received some water, and there was a guard who came with some of the younger people, and he had a vessel of something. Then they asked for more water, and they asked that the water be passed, but I don't know if we got any food the first day. As far as I know, nobody really mentioned any hunger, being hungry or needing food.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Maybe I did not get you quite well. I am talking not only of the first day in the tunnel, but the whole stay. What about food and drinking water during the whole stay inside tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was difficult there. You couldn't go out. If we received anything it had to be passed on, and it was a narrow space. So it was difficult. Somebody would receive some small piece of bread. You couldn't pass, you couldn't -- I don't know, but there was not much of that. Later maybe food was being given but nothing cooked at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Where did you sleep during the stay inside tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I was -- as you came in, I was to the left, maybe five or six metres away from the door. Later I can also say that those younger ones, who could move a bit more, they would move closer to the door, so that they would have more air and less of the stench that was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually the question was: where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sleep? I don't know. We just sat there and then there was no sleep. If you got a bit quiet, if you get some rest, you close your eyes a bit, but there was no sleeping. I don't know how to answer that question. We were in the same position day and night in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, did anybody take your valuables from prisoners after their arrest or after their arriving at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One evening, the third or the fourth day maybe, some people came, opened the door, and passed -- it was night, so as far as I could see it was like a soldier's helmet, and one person there was told, who was the person who was next to the door, whoever had something of any value, gold or watches, or something -- I apologise -- when it came to that point, there was very little that people had on them, because it had been taken away before, but that night whatever was left over, and it was -- people said that when they searched later, if they found something that these people will be responsible for it, that they would have to answer for that. Then this helmet was passed down the tunnel, and by chance I had a watch in a pocket. Had it been on my wrist, I probably would have taken it off. So I don't know how it -- I had it left on me. So my understanding was well, what do I know? So I gave it and it was passed around. I don't know how much was in there. It was night. I could hear when people were dropping something in it. So that's as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know who were these people who came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is a convenient point to stop now. It is 5.30. We shall continue with this witness tomorrow morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: -- at 10 o'clock. (5.30 pm)

procedural_notes.text: cross-examination by the defence, is it?
